To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

high (vs. low) issue involvement led to (a) greater opinion change in response to six (vs. two) arguments and a likable (unlikable) communicator, (b) greater content mediated (vs, source mediated) opinion persistence, and (c) greater use of message based (vs. source based) decision rules in explaining opinion change.
high involvement subjects show more opinion change given a large number of arguments, whereas low involvement recipients show more change given one argument from a likeable communicator.

(1) high involvement leads to greater opinion change in response to a greater number of arguments, whereas low involvement produces greater opinion change in reponse to a more likable communicator; (2) opinion change is more persistent when mediated by content based cognitions than when mediated by source based cognitions; and (3) the effects of communicator likability are more pronounced for low than for high involvement subjects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conditions under which people process messages systematically or heuristically, and with the implications of these processing strategies for message effects.
the effects of involvement on persuasion, and it is the first to show a main effect of communicator likeability for low involvement subjects.
the conditions under which message recipients use a heuristic or systematic processing strategy and the consequences of these processing strategies for opinion change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
high involvement leads to greater content mediated persuasion, whereas low in volvement leads to greater source mediated persuasion.

the results of the two experiments support the hypothesis that high involvement leads recipients to employ a message based systematic processing strategy in which source based cues are less important than content based cues, whereas low involvement recipients use a source based heuristic processing strategy in whch source based cues are more important than content based ones.
the results of this study support the notion that the processing strategies used by subjects to arrive at a decision are dependent on the level of involvement of the subjects in the decision.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
high involvement leads to systematic processing of message based information, whereas low involvement results in heuristic processing of source based information.
the effects of source versus message information on opinion change are mediated by the degree of involvement and the processing strategy employed.

the use of a heuristic processing strategy is more likely to lead to source mediated persuasion and less likely to lead to content mediated opinion change than is the use of a systematic processing strategy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of message versus source cues in persuasion is a function of involvement and that the effects of message versus source mediated persuasion differ in terms of persistence.
the effects of communicator and message characteristics on opinion change are mediated by the degree of involvement in the topic of the communication.
the effects of source versus message information in persuasion depend on the level of involvement of message recipients.
